questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

After the flood, the farmers complained that the [yield] from their rice fields had fallen sharply.
questions.explanation: In agriculture, "yield" is the amount of crop produced, that is, the harvest.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The bank manager advised the trader to open a [savings] account rather than keep cash under her mattress.
questions.explanation: A savings account is a deposit account in which money is kept to earn interest; the other options name different accounts or facilities.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The court [adjourned] the case to the first week of the next month.
questions.explanation: To adjourn a case is to postpone or suspend its hearing until a later date.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The doctor said the boy's fever was [symptomatic] of malaria.
questions.explanation: "Symptomatic of" means being a sign of, that is, indicative of, a disease.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The new governor promised to [prune] the size of the state cabinet.
questions.explanation: To prune is to cut back or reduce; the other options either change or remove the cabinet in other ways.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The journalist was praised for her [objective] report on the election.
questions.explanation: An objective report is fair and not influenced by personal feelings, that is, unbiased.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The senator's speech was so [verbose] that half the audience fell asleep.
questions.explanation: Verbose means using more words than needed, that is, long-winded; monotonous refers to tone, not wordiness.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The coach said the team's defeat was due to [complacency].
questions.explanation: Complacency is an uncritical satisfaction with oneself that leads to lack of effort.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The architect showed the clients a [blueprint] of the proposed hospital.
questions.explanation: A blueprint is a detailed technical plan or drawing of a building.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The principal's decision to expel the students was [arbitrary].
questions.explanation: An arbitrary decision is based on personal whim rather than reason or rule, hence unreasonable.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The mechanic said the car's engine needed a complete [overhaul].
questions.explanation: An overhaul is a thorough examination and repair of an engine or machine.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The pastor [admonished] the youths for coming late to the service.
questions.explanation: To admonish is to warn or reprove mildly, that is, to rebuke.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

Many villagers were [displaced] by the communal clash.
questions.explanation: Displaced people are forced out of their homes, that is, uprooted.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The minister's explanation only served to [obfuscate] the matter further.
questions.explanation: To obfuscate is to make something unclear or confusing; clarify is its opposite.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The tailor took the customer's [measurements] before cutting the fabric.
questions.explanation: In tailoring, measurements are the sizes of parts of the body.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The pilot announced that the aircraft would soon begin its [descent] into Kano.
questions.explanation: Descent in aviation is the downward movement of an aircraft towards landing.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The company's profits have been [dwindling] for three years.
questions.explanation: Dwindling means gradually becoming smaller; disappearing would mean vanishing completely.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The witness gave a [candid] account of what happened at the motor park.
questions.explanation: Candid means honest and straightforward, that is, frank.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The football club has [signed] a young striker from Enugu.
questions.explanation: In sport, to sign a player is to engage or recruit him under contract.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The pharmacist warned that the drug might cause [drowsiness].
questions.explanation: Drowsiness is the state of feeling sleepy.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The new classroom block is [spacious] and well lit.
questions.explanation: Spacious means having plenty of room; cramped means having too little room.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The lawyer argued that his client's confession was [voluntary].
questions.explanation: A voluntary act is done freely; a coerced one is obtained by force or threat.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

Her reply to the query was [terse].
questions.explanation: Terse means brief and abrupt; its opposite is lengthy.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The elders described the young chief as [magnanimous] in victory.
questions.explanation: Magnanimous means generous and forgiving, especially towards a rival; petty means small-minded and spiteful.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

Prices of foodstuffs have [risen] since the harvest ended.
questions.explanation: The opposite of risen is fallen.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The scientist's findings were regarded as [conclusive].
questions.explanation: Conclusive evidence settles a question; inconclusive evidence leaves it open.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

Ada is known for her [frugal] lifestyle.
questions.explanation: Frugal means sparing with money; extravagant means spending wastefully.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The patient's condition remained [stable] throughout the night.
questions.explanation: A stable condition is steady; a precarious one is unsteady and dangerous.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The guest speaker's lecture was [boring].
questions.explanation: Boring means dull; captivating means holding one's attention.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The committee's report was [ambiguous] on the issue of fees.
questions.explanation: Ambiguous means open to more than one interpretation; unequivocal means clear and leaving no doubt.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The rainfall this year has been [scanty].
questions.explanation: Scanty means too little; abundant means plentiful.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The suspect was [acquitted] by the High Court.
questions.explanation: To be acquitted is to be declared not guilty; to be convicted is to be found guilty.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The road to the village is [narrow].
questions.explanation: Narrow and broad are opposites in describing width.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

His colleagues found him [obsequious] towards the director.
questions.explanation: Obsequious means excessively eager to please; assertive means confident and forthright rather than fawning.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in [brackets].

The new manager adopted a [lenient] approach to latecoming.
questions.explanation: Lenient means tolerant or mild; strict is the opposite.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The patient was rushed to the ............ unit after the accident.
questions.explanation: The casualty unit (emergency department) receives accident victims; causality means cause and effect.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The ............ of the meeting were read and adopted before the agenda was discussed.
questions.explanation: The written record of a previous meeting is called the minutes; they are read and adopted at the next meeting.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The farmer used a ............ to spray his cocoa trees against black pod disease.
questions.explanation: A knapsack sprayer is carried on the back to apply chemicals to crops.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The goalkeeper made a brilliant ............ to keep the score at one-nil.
questions.explanation: In football a goalkeeper who stops a shot makes a save.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The accountant prepared a ............ to show what the business owned and owed at the end of the year.
questions.explanation: A balance sheet shows assets and liabilities at a given date.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the expression in [brackets].

When the results came out, Musa realised he had [bitten off more than he could chew] by registering for nine subjects.
options: eaten too much before the examination
taken on more than he could manage
questions.explanation: To bite off more than one can chew is to take on a task too big for one's ability.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the expression in [brackets].

The chairman told the members to [put their cards on the table].
questions.explanation: To put one's cards on the table is to be open and honest about one's plans or intentions.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the expression in [brackets].

My uncle is [a man of his word].
questions.explanation: A man of his word is a person who does what he promises.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the expression in [brackets].

The new policy is only [a drop in the ocean] compared with what is needed to fix the roads.
options: too small to make a real difference
questions.explanation: A drop in the ocean is an amount too small to have any real effect.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the expression in [brackets].

The two brothers have [buried the hatchet] after years of quarrelling over the land.
questions.explanation: To bury the hatchet is to end a quarrel and become friendly again.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the expression in [brackets].

The opposition party accused the government of [dragging its feet] on the new minimum wage.
questions.explanation: To drag one's feet is to be deliberately slow in doing something.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the expression in [brackets].

The trader [made a killing] during the festive season.
questions.explanation: To make a killing is to make a great deal of money quickly.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the expression in [brackets].

The headmaster [read the riot act] to the noisy pupils.
questions.explanation: To read the riot act is to give a severe warning to stop bad behaviour.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the expression in [brackets].

After the scandal, the councillor was [left holding the baby].
options: made to take the blame alone
questions.explanation: To be left holding the baby is to be left with responsibility or blame for something others started.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The students were asked to ............ attention to the instructions.
questions.explanation: The correct collocation is "pay attention".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The government has ............ a curfew in the troubled area.
questions.explanation: "Impose a curfew" is the standard collocation.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Despite the heavy rain, the match went ahead as ............
questions.explanation: "As scheduled" (as planned) is the fixed expression; the past participle is required.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The lawyer advised his client to ............ the offer of settlement out of court.
questions.explanation: To jump at an offer is to accept it eagerly.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The village head ............ a blind eye to the illegal felling of trees.
questions.explanation: The idiom is "turn a blind eye", meaning to pretend not to notice.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Bisi always ............ her best in every examination.
questions.explanation: The collocation is "do one's best".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The headmaster announced that the inter-house sports ............ on Friday.
questions.explanation: In reported speech after a past reporting verb, "will" shifts back to "would".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Chinedu said he ............ the film before, so he stayed at home.
questions.explanation: The earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

By the time the ambulance arrived, the injured man ............ a lot of blood.
questions.explanation: "By the time" + simple past in one clause calls for the past perfect in the other for the earlier action.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

If the rain had stopped earlier, the match ............
questions.explanation: A third conditional (had + past participle) pairs with "would have" + past participle.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Every member of the girls' choir must bring ............ uniform tomorrow.
questions.explanation: "Every member" is singular, and the choir is made up of girls, so "her" agrees with the antecedent.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The jury returned to the courtroom and took ............ seats one by one.
questions.explanation: Members acting individually ("one by one") make "jury" a plural antecedent here, so "their" is used.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Neither the principal nor the teachers knew what ............ were expected to do.
questions.explanation: With "neither ... nor", the pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent, "the teachers", which is plural.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The prefect was accused ............ stealing the class register.
questions.explanation: The verb "accuse" takes the preposition "of".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Kemi has been ill ............ last Tuesday.
questions.explanation: "Since" introduces a point in time with the present perfect; "for" introduces a period.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The new road will be a great relief ............ commuters.
questions.explanation: "A relief to" someone is the correct prepositional use.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The two communities have finally agreed ............ the terms of the peace accord.
questions.explanation: One agrees with a person, agrees to a proposal, and agrees on a matter to be settled such as terms.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Ngozi is very good ............ mathematics but poor ............ spelling.
questions.explanation: The idiomatic preposition after "good" and "poor" in referring to skills is "at".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The news of the plane crash was a dagger in the hearts of the families.
options: The news caused the families great pain.
The families were attacked with knives.
The families did not believe the news.
questions.explanation: The dagger is a metaphor for intense emotional pain.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

Our new class teacher runs the class with an iron hand.
options: She punishes pupils with a cane.
She is unfair to some pupils.
questions.explanation: "With an iron hand" means with firm, strict control.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

Ade is the black sheep of his family.
options: He is the darkest member of his family.
He is the only one who works.
He is regarded as a disgrace to his family.
questions.explanation: The black sheep is a member regarded as a disgrace or failure.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The opposition said the minister's promises were written in water.
options: The promises would not be kept.
The promises were made in a hurry.
questions.explanation: Something written in water does not last; the promises are empty.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

When the coach saw the score, his face fell.
options: He was hurt in the face.
questions.explanation: "His face fell" means his expression showed sudden disappointment.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The trader has a heart of gold.
questions.explanation: A heart of gold is a kind and generous nature.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The workers went on strike, and the hospital was a ghost town for a week.
options: Many patients died in the hospital.
The hospital was closed by the government.
questions.explanation: "A ghost town" figuratively describes a place almost empty of people.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

Tunde is burning the candle at both ends to prepare for the examination.
options: He is overworking himself, studying late and rising early.
He is studying two subjects at once.
questions.explanation: To burn the candle at both ends is to exhaust oneself by working from early till late.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The chairman's speech fell on deaf ears.
options: The audience could not hear him.
The audience were hard of hearing.
questions.explanation: Words that fall on deaf ears are ignored.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.

The new manager swept the office clean of lateness within a month.
options: He made the cleaners come early.
He eliminated the habit of lateness completely.
questions.explanation: "Swept clean of" figuratively means completely rid of.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The number of candidates who registered this year ............ higher than last year's.
questions.explanation: "The number of" takes a singular verb.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

A number of parents ............ complained about the new fees.
questions.explanation: "A number of" means "several" and takes a plural verb.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Mathematics ............ my best subject since I entered senior school.
questions.explanation: "Mathematics" is a singular subject name and "since" calls for the present perfect.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The furniture in the staff room ............ old and needs to be replaced.
questions.explanation: "Furniture" is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The police ............ investigating the matter.
questions.explanation: "Police" is a plural noun and takes a plural verb.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Bread and beans ............ my favourite breakfast.
questions.explanation: "Bread and beans" refers to a single dish, so it takes a singular verb.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

You have never been to Calabar, ............?
questions.explanation: A negative statement ("never") takes a positive tag: "have you?"

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Let's go to the library after lunch, ............?
questions.explanation: The tag for "Let's" is "shall we?"

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Nobody came to the meeting late, ............?
questions.explanation: "Nobody" is negative and takes the pronoun "they" in tags, so the tag is "did they?"

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

This is the ............ of the two routes to Abeokuta.
questions.explanation: The comparative is used when only two things are compared.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Of all the candidates interviewed, Amina was the ............
questions.explanation: The superlative is used for more than two; long adjectives form it with "most".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The more you practise, the ............ you will become.
questions.explanation: The construction "the more ... the + comparative" is used.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

We do not have ............ time left before the bus leaves.
questions.explanation: "Time" here is uncountable, so "much" is used in a negative sentence.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Only ............ students passed the test, so the teacher repeated the topic.
questions.explanation: "Students" is countable plural; "a few" means a small number.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Hardly had we arrived at the stadium ............ the rain started.
questions.explanation: "Hardly ... when" is the correct correlative pattern.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

No sooner had the referee blown the final whistle ............ the fans poured onto the pitch.
questions.explanation: "No sooner ... than" is the fixed correlative pattern.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

You will not be allowed in ............ you show your identity card.
questions.explanation: "Unless" means "if ... not" and introduces the condition.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

She is the girl ............ father owns the pharmacy.
questions.explanation: "Whose" is the possessive relative pronoun.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The man ............ the police arrested yesterday has been released.
questions.explanation: "Whom" is the object of "arrested" in the relative clause.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

I would rather you ............ the money to me tomorrow.
questions.explanation: "Would rather" + a different subject takes the past (subjunctive) form for present or future meaning.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

It is high time the government ............ the roads in this area.
questions.explanation: "It is high time" is followed by the past tense form.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The thief was caught ............ he was climbing the fence.
questions.explanation: "While" introduces a clause of simultaneous time; "during" is a preposition and cannot take a clause.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Ibrahim is taller ............ his elder brother.
questions.explanation: Comparatives are followed by "than".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The visitors have been waiting ............ two hours.
questions.explanation: "For" introduces a period of time.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Had I known about the strike, I ............ the journey.
questions.explanation: The inverted conditional "Had I known" is a third conditional and takes "would have" + past participle.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The house ............ by the time the fire service arrived.
questions.explanation: Passive past perfect is needed for an action completed before another past action.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Each of the boys ............ given a new textbook.
questions.explanation: "Each" is singular and takes a singular verb.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Neither of the two answers ............ correct.
questions.explanation: "Neither of" takes a singular verb in formal English.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The scissors ............ on the table where you left them.
questions.explanation: "Scissors" is a plural-form noun and takes a plural verb.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Not only the students but also the principal ............ invited to the ceremony.
questions.explanation: With "not only ... but also", the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "the principal".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Please, give me ............ umbrella on the chair.
questions.explanation: A specific umbrella is identified ("on the chair"), so the definite article is used.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

She has been ............ honest woman all her life.
questions.explanation: "Honest" begins with a vowel sound because the h is silent, so "an" is used.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

My father bought ............ for the new sitting room.
questions.explanation: "Furniture" is uncountable and has no plural form.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The ............ were asked to submit their reports before the end of the month.
questions.explanation: In compound nouns of this kind the main noun, "editor", takes the plural.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The lecture was so ............ that many students left early.
questions.explanation: The -ing adjective describes the thing causing the feeling.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The workers were ............ by the management's refusal to pay them.
questions.explanation: The -ed adjective describes the people experiencing the feeling.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Scarcely ............ the hall when the lights went out.
questions.explanation: After "scarcely" at the beginning of a sentence, the auxiliary is inverted: "had we entered".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The children ............ playing in the field when it began to rain.
questions.explanation: The past continuous with a plural subject requires "were".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

He is used to ............ early every morning.
questions.explanation: "Be used to" is followed by the -ing form.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Our teacher made us ............ the essay again.
questions.explanation: "Make" in the active voice is followed by the bare infinitive.

questions.stem: Choose the word that contains the sound /θ/.
questions.explanation: "Thumb" begins with /θ/; "Thomas" and "thyme" begin with /t/, while "this" and "clothe" have the voiced /ð/.

questions.stem: Choose the word in which "ch" has the same sound as in "chef".
questions.explanation: In "chef" and "machine", "ch" is /ʃ/; "church" and "chess" have /tʃ/, "character" and "choir" have /k/.

questions.stem: Choose the word that contains the sound /ʒ/.
questions.explanation: "Measure" has /ʒ/; "pressure" and "sure" have /ʃ/, "major" and "cage" have /dʒ/.

questions.stem: In which of the following words is the letter "b" silent?
questions.explanation: In "plumber" the b is not pronounced; in the others it is.

questions.stem: In which of the following words is the letter "k" silent?
questions.explanation: Initial "k" before "n" is silent, as in "knowledge".

When Halima first suggested that her secondary school in Bauchi should collect plastic bottles, her classmates laughed. The bottles were everywhere: in the gutters, behind the dining hall, floating in the stream that ran past the school farm. Nobody, they said, would pay good money for rubbish.

Halima did not argue. Instead she spent a weekend visiting the small recycling depot near the motor park, where a young man named Sani bought bottles by the kilogram and pressed them into bales for a factory in Kano. He told her the price, showed her how the bottles had to be sorted and promised to send his tricycle to the school every fortnight if she could fill twenty sacks.

The first collection was humiliating. After two weeks of effort, Halima and three friends had filled only six sacks, and Sani's driver went away grumbling. But the second fortnight was different. The principal, who had seen the girls picking bottles out of the gutter in the rain, announced at assembly that the money from the bottles would buy new balls for the games department. By the end of the term, every class had a collection box, the gutters were clear, and the stream behind the farm ran clean for the first time in years.

Halima says the money was never the point. "People think a problem is too big because they are looking at all of it at once," she explains. "We only looked at one bottle at a time."

Why did Halima's classmates laugh at her suggestion?
options: They thought nobody would pay for used bottles.
They thought she was too young to lead.
They had never seen plastic bottles.
They thought the principal would forbid it.
They thought the depot was too far away.
questions.explanation: The passage says they believed nobody "would pay good money for rubbish".

Read the passage below and answer the question that follows.

For most of the past century, the people of many rural communities in Nigeria have waited for electricity to come to them along wires from distant power stations. In many places it never came, or it came so irregularly that it was hardly worth having. Today a different idea is gaining ground: instead of waiting for the grid, communities are generating their own power from the sun.

The principle is simple. Panels made of silicon convert sunlight into electric current, which charges batteries during the day. In the evening the stored power lights homes, runs fans and keeps refrigerators cold. A cluster of panels serving a whole village, called a mini-grid, can power a clinic, a grinding mill and a school at a fraction of the cost of extending the national grid over long distances.

The benefits are not only economic. A nurse who no longer delivers babies by the light of a kerosene lantern works more safely. Pupils who can read after dark perform better in examinations. Traders who can keep fish and drinks cold earn more and waste less.

There are difficulties, of course. The initial cost of panels and batteries is high, and batteries must be replaced every few years. Panels that are not cleaned of dust lose much of their efficiency, and equipment is sometimes stolen. Experts insist that solar projects succeed only where the community itself is involved in planning and maintenance, so that the people see the system as their own and not as a gift that someone else must look after.

According to the passage, what is the "different idea" that is gaining ground?
options: Communities producing their own electricity from sunlight
questions.explanation: The passage says communities are "generating their own power from the sun".

For most of the past century, the people of many rural communities in Nigeria have waited for electricity to come to them along wires from distant power stations. In many places it never came, or it came so irregularly that it was hardly worth having. Today a different idea is gaining ground: instead of waiting for the grid, communities are generating their own power from the sun.

The principle is simple. Panels made of silicon convert sunlight into electric current, which charges batteries during the day. In the evening the stored power lights homes, runs fans and keeps refrigerators cold. A cluster of panels serving a whole village, called a mini-grid, can power a clinic, a grinding mill and a school at a fraction of the cost of extending the national grid over long distances.

The benefits are not only economic. A nurse who no longer delivers babies by the light of a kerosene lantern works more safely. Pupils who can read after dark perform better in examinations. Traders who can keep fish and drinks cold earn more and waste less.

There are difficulties, of course. The initial cost of panels and batteries is high, and batteries must be replaced every few years. Panels that are not cleaned of dust lose much of their efficiency, and equipment is sometimes stolen. Experts insist that solar projects succeed only where the community itself is involved in planning and maintenance, so that the people see the system as their own and not as a gift that someone else must look after.

questions.explanation: The writer praises its benefits but also sets out its difficulties.

Read the passage below and answer the question that follows.

Road accidents claim thousands of lives on Nigerian highways every year, and most of them could be prevented. The commonest cause is excessive speed. A driver travelling too fast has less time to react to a pothole, a broken-down lorry or a pedestrian, and when a collision happens at high speed, the injuries are far more severe.

Closely linked to speeding is dangerous overtaking. Many drivers, impatient behind slow trucks, pull out on bends or near the top of hills where they cannot see oncoming vehicles. Head-on collisions, the deadliest of all crashes, are often the result.

The condition of vehicles also plays a part. Tyres worn smooth, faulty brakes and broken headlamps turn an ordinary journey into a gamble. Some commercial vehicles are loaded far beyond their capacity, which makes them hard to steer and to stop.

Finally, the human body has limits that many drivers ignore. Drivers who work for long hours without rest become drowsy, and a few seconds of sleep at the wheel can be fatal. Alcohol and certain drugs slow reactions and cloud judgement in the same way.

The solutions are well known. Speed limits should be enforced, vehicles should be inspected regularly, and drivers should be trained and tested properly before they are licensed. Above all, every road user must accept that safety is a personal responsibility and not only the duty of the authorities.

Which of the following best summarises the first paragraph?
options: Thousands of people die on Nigerian roads every year.
Pedestrians are careless on the highways.
Excessive speed is the commonest cause of road accidents.
High-speed collisions cause severe injuries to drivers only.
questions.explanation: The paragraph's main point is that excessive speed is the commonest cause.

questions.stem:
Students in your school now spend long hours in the computer laboratory without supervision, and some have been damaging the equipment. Write a letter to your Principal drawing attention to the problem and suggesting ways of protecting the laboratory.

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.) [50 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — statement of the problem (unsupervised use, examples of damage such as broken keyboards, viruses, missing mice); effects on learning and cost to the school; at least three practical suggestions (rota of supervisors, logbook, passwords, CCTV or locks, ICT club monitors, penalties); polite appeal for action
10 marks: Organisation — writer's address and date; receiver's (Principal's) address; formal salutation (Dear Sir/Madam); heading in capitals or underlined; introduction stating purpose; logical paragraphs; conclusion; "Yours faithfully", signature and full name
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and smooth flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: A formal letter. After the addresses and "Dear Sir," a heading such as "PROTECTING OUR COMPUTER LABORATORY" introduces the purpose. The body describes the problem with examples (keyboards pulled apart, games installed that spread viruses, chairs broken), explains its effect on lessons and on the school's finances, and suggests remedies: a teacher on duty during free periods, a sign-in book, user passwords, rules displayed on the wall, a student monitors' committee and sanctions for offenders. It ends by thanking the Principal and closes with "Yours faithfully", signature and full name.

10 marks: Organisation — writer's address and date only; informal salutation (Dear Femi); friendly introduction; well-arranged paragraphs, one piece of advice per paragraph; conclusion with good wishes; informal close (Your loving cousin) and first name
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and smooth flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: An informal letter opening with greetings and congratulations on the admission. It reassures the cousin that the first weeks are hard for everyone, then advises: choose friends who are serious about their studies; obey school rules; plan the day so that prep time is used well; keep clothes and provisions labelled and locked; respect seniors but report any bullying to the housemaster; join a club; write home regularly. It closes with encouragement, regards to the family and "Your loving cousin, Ada".

Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

Old Pa Okonkwo had been the village carpenter for as long as anyone could remember. His workshop, a low shed roofed with rusty zinc, stood at the junction where the road from the market met the path to the stream, and from dawn until the light failed the sound of his plane on wood could be heard by everybody who passed.

When the new furniture shop opened in town, with its shining glass front and its sofas wrapped in plastic, people said that Pa Okonkwo was finished. Who would wait three weeks for a hand-made chair when a factory one could be carried home the same afternoon? For a while it seemed they were right. The orders dried up, and the old man spent long hours sitting on a bench outside his shed, whittling small animals for the children.

Then the rains came. Within one season, the bright factory chairs in half the houses of the village had begun to sag. Their legs, made of soft wood glued together, swelled and cracked in the damp. One by one, their owners carried them, a little shamefaced, down the road to the junction.

Pa Okonkwo did not gloat. He mended what could be mended and quietly told the owners which could not. Within a year, his shed was busier than it had ever been, and he had taken on two apprentices, his own grandson among them. "A chair," he liked to say, running a thumb along a joint he had cut, "is a promise. The cheap ones break their promises."

(a) Where exactly was Pa Okonkwo's workshop? [2 marks]
(b) Why did people think the old man was "finished"? [2 marks]
(c) What happened to the factory chairs during the rainy season, and why? [2 marks]
(d) Why were the owners of the chairs "a little shamefaced"? [2 marks]
(e) What does Pa Okonkwo mean when he says that a chair "is a promise"? [2 marks]
(f) "when a factory one could be carried home the same afternoon" (i) What grammatical name is given to this expression? (ii) What is its function? [2 marks]
(g) "The orders dried up" (i) What figure of speech is contained in this expression? (ii) What does it mean? [2 marks]
(h) For each of the following words, find another word or phrase which means the same and can replace it as it is used in the passage: (i) shining (ii) sag (iii) swelled (iv) gloat (v) mended (vi) busier [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) at the junction where the road from the market met the path to the stream
2 marks: (b) a new furniture shop had opened in town selling factory-made furniture that could be bought and taken home at once, while his took weeks
2 marks: (c) they sagged and their legs swelled and cracked (1) because they were made of soft wood glued together and the damp affected them (1)
2 marks: (d) they had abandoned the old carpenter for the shop, and now had to go back to him for help
2 marks: (e) a good chair should be dependable and last as its maker intends; quality work keeps faith with the buyer (any reasonable interpretation)
2 marks: (f) (i) adverbial clause of time (1); (ii) it modifies the verb "wait" (1)
2 marks: (g) (i) metaphor (1); (ii) the orders stopped coming / became very few (1)
6 marks: (h) one mark each: (i) gleaming / bright (ii) sink / droop (iii) expanded / bulged (iv) boast / rejoice at their misfortune (v) repaired / fixed (vi) more active / fuller of work
questions.explanation: (a) At the junction of the market road and the path to the stream. (b) Because a modern furniture shop had opened offering ready-made chairs. (c) They sagged, swelled and cracked because of soft, glued wood in the damp. (d) They had abandoned him and now needed him. (e) A well-made chair can be relied upon. (f) Adverbial clause of time modifying "wait". (g) Metaphor: orders stopped coming. (h) gleaming; droop; expanded; boast; repaired; more active.

questions.stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

It is a curious fact that the people who complain most about noise are often those who produce the most of it. Walk down any busy street in a Nigerian city and you will hear the result: generators roaring in front of shops, loudspeakers advertising medicines and music, drivers leaning on their horns as if the sound alone could clear the traffic ahead. Yet ask any of these people what they dislike about city life, and many will name the noise.

Scientists who study sound measure it in decibels. Normal conversation is about sixty decibels; a busy road may reach eighty-five; a generator at close range can easily exceed ninety. Prolonged exposure to sound above eighty-five decibels is known to damage hearing, and the damage is permanent, because the tiny hair cells in the inner ear that are destroyed by loud noise do not grow back.

Hearing loss is only the most obvious harm. Constant noise raises stress levels, disturbs sleep and makes it harder for children to concentrate in class. Teachers in schools beside major roads often have to stop in the middle of a sentence and wait for a lorry to pass.

Some cities have passed laws against noise from places of worship, clubs and generators, but enforcement is weak, partly because noise is so common that people no longer notice it. Perhaps the first step is simply to listen: to stand still for a minute in a busy place and pay attention to what our ears are enduring.

(a) What is the "curious fact" mentioned at the beginning of the passage? [2 marks]
(b) Name two sources of noise mentioned in the first paragraph. [2 marks]
(c) Why is hearing loss caused by loud noise permanent? [2 marks]
(d) Apart from hearing loss, state two other effects of constant noise mentioned in the passage. [2 marks]
(e) Why, according to the writer, are laws against noise poorly enforced? [2 marks]
(f) "as if the sound alone could clear the traffic ahead" (i) What grammatical name is given to this expression? (ii) What is its function? [2 marks]
(g) What is the writer's attitude to people who complain about noise? Give a reason for your answer. [2 marks]
(h) For each of the following words, find another word or phrase which means the same and can replace it as it is used in the passage: (i) curious (ii) roaring (iii) prolonged (iv) disturbs (v) weak (vi) enduring [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) the people who complain most about noise are often the ones who make the most of it
2 marks: (b) any two: generators; loudspeakers advertising medicines and music; drivers' horns (1 each)
2 marks: (c) loud noise destroys the tiny hair cells in the inner ear, and these cells do not grow back
2 marks: (d) any two: it raises stress; it disturbs sleep; it makes it hard for children to concentrate in class (1 each)
2 marks: (e) noise is so common that people no longer notice it
2 marks: (f) (i) adverbial clause of manner (1); (ii) it modifies the verb phrase "leaning on their horns" (1)
2 marks: (g) mildly critical / ironical (1): they complain while producing the noise themselves (1)
6 marks: (h) one mark each: (i) strange / odd (ii) thundering / blaring (iii) long / extended (iv) disrupts / interrupts (v) lax / ineffective (vi) suffering / bearing
questions.explanation: (a) Those who complain most about noise often produce the most. (b) Generators; loudspeakers. (c) The inner-ear hair cells destroyed do not grow back. (d) Stress; disturbed sleep. (e) People are so used to noise that they do not notice it. (f) Adverbial clause of manner modifying "leaning on their horns". (g) Ironical/critical because the complainers make the noise. (h) strange; blaring; long; disrupts; lax; bearing.

questions.stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

My father believed that a journey should begin before the sun did. So it was that at four o'clock on a cold Harmattan morning, my two brothers and I were bundled, half asleep, into the back of his old station wagon for the long drive from Ilorin to our grandmother's village near Ogbomoso.

For the first hour nobody spoke. The headlamps carved a narrow tunnel out of the darkness, and dust hung in the beams like smoke. Then, as the sky over the savannah turned from black to grey and from grey to a pale, washed-out gold, my father began to sing. He had a terrible voice, and he knew it, but he sang the old songs his own father had taught him, and after a while my youngest brother, who was only six, began to clap.

We reached the village just as the women were returning from the stream with pots balanced on their heads. Our grandmother was waiting at the door of her compound, leaning on a stick that she did not really need. She held each of us at arm's length, examined us as if we were yams at the market, and declared that we were far too thin. Then she disappeared into the kitchen, from which, for the rest of the day, came smells that made the long journey worth every minute.

(a) Why did the family set out at four o'clock in the morning? [2 marks]
(b) Describe the scene the travellers saw during the first hour of the journey. [2 marks]
(c) Why do you think the father continued singing although he "had a terrible voice"? [2 marks]
(d) What does the writer suggest by saying that the grandmother leaned "on a stick that she did not really need"? [2 marks]
(e) What did the grandmother's comment that the children were "far too thin" lead her to do? [2 marks]
(f) "who was only six" (i) What grammatical name is given to this expression? (ii) What is its function? [2 marks]
(g) "examined us as if we were yams at the market" (i) What figure of speech is this? (ii) What does it suggest about the grandmother? [2 marks]
(h) For each of the following words, find another word or phrase which means the same and can replace it as it is used in the passage: (i) bundled (ii) carved (iii) pale (iv) declared (v) disappeared (vi) worth [6 marks]

questions.stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

Every September, millions of parents across Nigeria face the same arithmetic: school fees, uniforms, textbooks, transport. For many, the textbooks are the hardest item to afford, and so a thriving trade has grown up in second-hand books. At the roadside stalls near large schools, a well-used copy of a chemistry text may sell for a third of the price of a new one, its margins crowded with the notes of earlier owners.

Some educationists frown on this trade. Old editions, they argue, may contain outdated information, and pages are often missing. Yet for a pupil who would otherwise have no book at all, a battered copy is a treasure. The more serious problem is the pirated book, printed cheaply from photographs of the original, which robs authors and publishers of their income and is often so blurred that diagrams are unreadable.

A few schools have found a sensible middle way. At the end of each session, they ask outgoing students to donate their books to a school bank, from which incoming students borrow them for a small fee. The fees pay for replacements, and the books, carefully checked, remain in use for many years. Such schemes cost little, but they depend on something money cannot buy: a sense among students that what they leave behind will help someone else.

(a) Why are textbooks described as "the hardest item to afford"? [2 marks]
(b) State two objections that some educationists raise against second-hand books. [2 marks]
(c) Why, according to the writer, is the pirated book a more serious problem? [2 marks]
(d) How does the school book bank remain in operation for many years? [2 marks]
(e) What is the "something money cannot buy" mentioned in the last sentence? [2 marks]
(f) "which robs authors and publishers of their income" (i) What grammatical name is given to this expression? (ii) What is its function? [2 marks]
(g) "a battered copy is a treasure" (i) What figure of speech is used? (ii) What does it mean? [2 marks]
(h) For each of the following words, find another word or phrase which means the same and can replace it as it is used in the passage: (i) thriving (ii) crowded (iii) frown on (iv) outdated (v) sensible (vi) donate [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) they are expensive compared with other school needs, and parents must buy many at once
2 marks: (b) old editions may contain outdated information (1); pages are often missing (1)
2 marks: (c) it robs authors and publishers of income (1) and is often too blurred to read, especially the diagrams (1)
2 marks: (d) students borrow books for a small fee, which pays for replacements, and the books are carefully checked
2 marks: (e) a spirit of generosity / concern for others among students
2 marks: (f) (i) adjectival (relative) clause (1); (ii) it qualifies the noun "book" (the pirated book) (1)
2 marks: (g) (i) metaphor (1); (ii) even a damaged book is very valuable to a pupil who has none (1)
6 marks: (h) one mark each: (i) flourishing / booming (ii) filled / packed (iii) disapprove of (iv) out of date / obsolete (v) reasonable / wise (vi) give / hand over freely
questions.explanation: (a) They cost a lot relative to other needs. (b) Outdated information; missing pages. (c) It deprives authors and publishers and is often unreadable. (d) The borrowing fees fund replacements and books are checked. (e) Concern for others. (f) Adjectival clause qualifying "book". (g) Metaphor: a worn book is precious to a pupil without one. (h) flourishing; filled; disapprove of; obsolete; wise; give.

questions.stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

The first thing Emeka noticed about the new boy was his shoes. They were the wrong kind, black leather ones with laces, when everybody in Class Two wore brown sandals. The second thing he noticed was that the boy did not seem to care.

His name was Tobi, and his family had just moved from Lagos because his mother had been posted to the general hospital in the town. In class he answered questions quietly and correctly, and at break he sat alone under the mango tree reading a book with a torn cover. Some of the boys began to call him "Lagos Shoes", and Emeka, to his later shame, laughed with them.

It was the inter-house football match that changed things. Emeka's house was a player short, and the games master, looking around in desperation, pointed at Tobi. The boys groaned. But within ten minutes of the start, Tobi, still in his black shoes, had dribbled past three defenders and scored. By the end of the match he had scored twice more, and the boys who had mocked him were carrying him on their shoulders.

That evening, walking home, Emeka fell into step beside him and asked, a little awkwardly, what book he had been reading under the mango tree. Tobi grinned and handed it over. It was a book about football.

(a) Why did Emeka notice Tobi's shoes? [2 marks]
(b) Why had Tobi's family moved to the town? [2 marks]
(c) How did Emeka feel later about having laughed at Tobi? Quote the words that show it. [2 marks]
(d) Why did the boys groan when the games master chose Tobi? [2 marks]
(e) What is surprising about the book Tobi had been reading? [2 marks]
(f) "looking around in desperation" (i) What grammatical name is given to this expression? (ii) What is its function? [2 marks]
(g) What does the change in the boys' behaviour after the match suggest about them? [2 marks]
(h) For each of the following words, find another word or phrase which means the same and can replace it as it is used in the passage: (i) posted (ii) quietly (iii) mocked (iv) awkwardly (v) grinned (vi) desperation [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) they were black leather shoes with laces, unlike the brown sandals everybody else wore
2 marks: (b) his mother had been posted to the general hospital in the town
2 marks: (c) he was ashamed (1); "to his later shame" (1)
2 marks: (d) they did not expect him to play well / they regarded him as an outsider
2 marks: (e) it was about football, which explains his skill / links his quiet reading to the talent he showed
2 marks: (f) (i) participial phrase (1); (ii) it qualifies/describes "the games master" (adjectival function) (1)
2 marks: (g) they judged by appearance and changed their attitude once he showed ability / they were fickle (any reasonable answer)
6 marks: (h) one mark each: (i) transferred / sent (ii) softly / calmly (iii) ridiculed / laughed at (iv) shyly / uneasily (v) smiled broadly (vi) despair / hopelessness
questions.explanation: (a) They were black leather lace-ups unlike everyone's sandals. (b) His mother was posted to the hospital there. (c) Ashamed: "to his later shame". (d) They expected him to play badly. (e) It was about football. (f) Participial phrase qualifying "the games master". (g) They judged by appearance and changed when he showed talent. (h) transferred; calmly; ridiculed; uneasily; smiled broadly; despair.

questions.stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

Water is often called the most precious resource on earth, and yet in many of our towns it is treated as if it were the cheapest. Public taps run all night because nobody bothers to close them. Burst pipes along the main roads send clear water flowing into gutters for weeks before they are repaired. In private homes, people leave the tap open while brushing their teeth or washing plates, and cars are washed with a running hose instead of a bucket.

Meanwhile, in the same towns, women and children walk long distances before dawn to queue at boreholes, and water vendors push their carts from street to street selling twenty-litre jerrycans at prices that rise sharply in the dry season. The contrast could hardly be sharper: abundance wasted on one side, scarcity endured on the other.

Part of the problem is that water rarely carries its true cost. Where supply is free or charged at a flat rate, users have little reason to save it. Metering, by which each household pays for what it uses, has reduced waste wherever it has been properly introduced. But metering alone cannot change habits that have been formed over a lifetime. Children who learn at school to close a dripping tap, and who see their parents do the same, are more likely to grow into adults who value what flows from the pipe.

(a) In what sense is water treated "as if it were the cheapest" resource? [2 marks]
(b) Give two examples of the waste of water in private homes. [2 marks]
(c) What is the "contrast" described in the second paragraph? [2 marks]
(d) Why do users have little reason to save water where it is free or charged at a flat rate? [2 marks]
(e) Why, according to the writer, is metering alone not enough? [2 marks]
(f) "by which each household pays for what it uses" (i) What grammatical name is given to this expression? (ii) What is its function? [2 marks]
(g) "abundance wasted on one side, scarcity endured on the other" (i) What figure of speech is used? (ii) Explain it. [2 marks]
(h) For each of the following words, find another word or phrase which means the same and can replace it as it is used in the passage: (i) precious (ii) bothers (iii) queue (iv) sharply (v) properly (vi) value [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) it is wasted carelessly, as if it cost nothing
2 marks: (b) any two: leaving the tap running while brushing teeth or washing plates; washing cars with a running hose (1 each)
2 marks: (c) some people waste plenty of water while others suffer from shortage and pay dearly for it
2 marks: (d) they pay the same however much they use, so saving brings them no benefit
2 marks: (e) it cannot change long-formed habits; children must learn to value water at school and from their parents
2 marks: (f) (i) adjectival (relative) clause (1); (ii) it qualifies the noun "metering" (1)
2 marks: (g) (i) antithesis (contrast) (1); (ii) opposite situations are set side by side: waste of plenty and suffering from lack (1)
6 marks: (h) one mark each: (i) valuable (ii) takes the trouble (iii) line up / wait in line (iv) steeply / greatly (v) correctly (vi) treasure / appreciate
questions.explanation: (a) It is wasted as though it cost nothing. (b) Running taps while brushing teeth; washing cars with a hose. (c) Waste of plenty beside painful scarcity. (d) Their bills do not change with use. (e) Habits need education at school and home. (f) Adjectival clause qualifying "metering". (g) Antithesis contrasting waste and lack. (h) valuable; takes the trouble; line up; steeply; correctly; appreciate.

Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

Many people imagine that the secret of success in examinations is long hours of reading the night before. In truth, the students who do best are usually those who have learnt to study wisely throughout the year.

The first habit of such students is regular revision. Instead of leaving everything until the last minute, they go over each day's lessons the same evening, when the material is still fresh. A short review on the day of learning saves hours of relearning later.

They also plan their time. A simple timetable that shares the week among all the subjects, with more time for the difficult ones, prevents a student from reading only the subjects he enjoys.

Successful students are active rather than passive readers. They do not merely stare at their notes; they make summaries, draw diagrams, test themselves with past questions and explain topics to their friends. Teaching others is one of the surest ways to discover what one has not understood.

Equally important is the care of the body. A tired brain learns little, so good students sleep for enough hours, eat properly and take some exercise. Many of them also avoid reading in noisy places, choosing quiet corners where they can concentrate.

Finally, they are not ashamed to ask for help. When a topic defeats them, they consult their teachers or classmates at once instead of hoping it will not appear in the examination.

In six sentences, one for each, summarise the habits of successful students as described in the passage. [30 marks]

5 marks: They plan their time with a timetable covering all subjects. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: They read actively, making summaries, diagrams and testing themselves. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: They explain or teach topics to others. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: They take care of their bodies through enough sleep, good food and exercise / they study in quiet places. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: They ask for help promptly when they do not understand. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)

They teach topics to their friends. 5. They look after their health and study in quiet places. 6. They seek help quickly when a topic is difficult.

Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

Trees are among the most useful things in our environment, and yet they are cut down every day with hardly a thought. A walk through any farming area will show the stumps where forests once stood.

Trees protect the soil. Their roots bind the earth together, and their leaves break the force of heavy rain. Where trees are cleared on slopes, the topsoil is quickly washed away, leaving gullies that can swallow roads and houses.

They also influence the weather. Through their leaves, trees release large amounts of water vapour into the air, which helps to form rain clouds. In the north of the country, belts of trees slow the dry winds that carry sand southwards and help to hold back the desert.

Trees provide food, medicine and income. Fruit trees such as mango, orange and cashew feed millions of families, and the bark and leaves of many trees are used in traditional medicine. Timber and other products give work to carpenters, traders and transporters.

Moreover, trees absorb carbon dioxide, one of the gases responsible for global warming, and give out oxygen.

To keep these benefits, cutting must be controlled. Every tree felled should be replaced by planting at least one more, and communities should protect forest reserves from illegal loggers. Schools can help by setting up tree-planting clubs.

(a) In four sentences, one for each, summarise the benefits of trees mentioned in the passage. [20 marks]
(b) In two sentences, one for each, summarise the measures the writer recommends for protecting trees. [10 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a)(i) Trees prevent soil erosion. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (a)(ii) Trees help to bring rain and check desert encroachment. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (a)(iii) Trees provide food, medicine and income / employment. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (a)(iv) Trees absorb carbon dioxide and give out oxygen. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (b)(i) Every tree cut down should be replaced by planting / tree-cutting should be controlled. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (b)(ii) Forest reserves should be protected from illegal loggers / schools should set up tree-planting clubs. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
questions.explanation: (a) Trees prevent soil erosion. They help to bring rain and check the desert. They provide food, medicine and jobs. They absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen. (b) Every tree felled should be replaced. Forest reserves should be protected and schools should form tree-planting clubs.

Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions on it.

The mobile phone has changed the way Nigerians live and work more quickly than perhaps any other invention. Twenty-five years ago, a telephone line was a luxury that took months to obtain. Today even petty traders in remote markets carry phones, and the effects are visible everywhere.

For business, the change has been enormous. A farmer in Benue can call buyers in Lagos to compare prices before he sells his yams, instead of accepting whatever the middleman offers. Artisans advertise their services on social media and receive orders from customers they have never met.

Banking has also been transformed. Millions of people who have never stepped into a banking hall now send and receive money through their phones, pay bills and buy airtime with a few taps.

In emergencies, phones save lives. A driver who witnesses a crash can summon help at once, and families can be warned of floods or unrest.

The benefits, however, come with costs. Fraudsters use phones to trick the unwary into revealing their bank details. Many young people spend so much time on their phones that their studies and relationships suffer. And drivers who make calls or send messages while driving cause accidents that could easily have been avoided.

(a) In three sentences, one for each, summarise the benefits of the mobile phone mentioned in the passage. [15 marks]
(b) In three sentences, one for each, summarise the problems associated with the mobile phone. [15 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a)(i) It has made business easier, enabling people to compare prices and reach customers. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (a)(ii) It allows people to carry out banking transactions without going to a bank. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (a)(iii) It helps to summon help and give warnings in emergencies. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (b)(i) Fraudsters use it to cheat people. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (b)(ii) Excessive use harms young people's studies and relationships. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (b)(iii) Using phones while driving causes accidents. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
questions.explanation: (a) It makes business easier. It enables banking without visiting banks. It brings quick help in emergencies. (b) Fraudsters use it to cheat people. Overuse harms young people's studies and relationships. Phoning while driving causes accidents.

Every year, thousands of young Nigerians leave secondary school without the skills that employers or self-employment require. One of the best answers to this problem is vocational training, which teaches practical trades such as tailoring, carpentry, welding, catering and electrical installation.

Vocational training offers a quick route to earning a living. A young person who masters a trade can begin to work within a year or two, without waiting for the many years of study that a university degree demands.

It also reduces unemployment and the crime that often follows idleness. A youth who is busy in a workshop and proud of his skill is less likely to be drawn into armed robbery or internet fraud.

Furthermore, the nation needs these skills. Many buildings are wired by unqualified electricians and many cars are repaired by people with no formal training, sometimes with dangerous results. Skilled technicians would raise the standard of such work.

Unfortunately, many parents still look down on trades and insist that their children go to university, whatever their talents. In addition, many technical colleges lack equipment and qualified instructors.

If vocational training is to fulfil its promise, government must equip technical colleges properly, and parents and the media must stop treating skilled work as second-best.

(a) In three sentences, one for each, summarise the advantages of vocational training. [15 marks]
(b) In three sentences, one for each, summarise the problems facing vocational training and the solutions the writer proposes. [15 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a)(i) It enables young people to start earning a living quickly. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (a)(ii) It reduces unemployment and crime. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (a)(iii) It supplies skills the nation needs and raises standards of work. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (b)(i) Many parents look down on trades / prefer university for their children. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (b)(ii) Many technical colleges lack equipment and qualified instructors. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: (b)(iii) Government should equip technical colleges, and parents and the media should respect skilled work. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)

Technical colleges lack equipment and instructors. Government should equip the colleges and society should value skilled work.

It is easy to forget, in an age of mobile phones and the internet, how much the ordinary town library once meant to people who could not afford to buy books. Yet libraries remain as valuable today as they ever were, though for somewhat different reasons.

A good library gives everyone, rich or poor, access to knowledge. Students who cannot buy expensive textbooks can read them there, and adults can borrow books on farming, health or business without paying.

Libraries also provide a quiet place to study. In crowded homes where several children share a room and the television is always on, the reading room of a library may be the only place where a student can concentrate.

Modern libraries do more than lend books. Many now offer free access to computers and the internet, and librarians help users to search for reliable information and to tell it apart from rumour and falsehood.

Furthermore, libraries bring communities together. Reading clubs, story hours for children, lectures and exhibitions turn them into centres of local life.

Sadly, many public libraries in our towns are in poor condition, with old books, leaking roofs and irregular power. They deserve better funding, and their staff deserve training in the new technology.

Using one sentence for each, summarise in five sentences the reasons why libraries remain valuable, according to the passage. [25 marks]
In one sentence, state what the writer thinks should be done about public libraries. [5 marks]

Many people regard the market as merely a place to buy and sell, but in Nigerian towns and villages it has always been much more than that.

Above all, the market is the centre of trade. Farmers bring their produce there and buy the goods they cannot make themselves, and prices are set by the meeting of buyers and sellers.

It is also a place of social contact. Friends and relatives from different villages meet there on market days, exchange news, arrange marriages and settle small quarrels.

The market spreads information. Before radio and telephones reached the villages, it was in the market that people heard about deaths, festivals and the decisions of the chiefs, and to a large extent this is still true.

In addition, it provides employment for many who are not traders, including porters, drivers, food sellers and money changers.

Finally, many markets have a religious and cultural significance. Some are associated with particular deities, and festivals often begin or end there.

Using one sentence for each, summarise the functions of the market in Nigerian towns and villages according to the passage. [25 marks]
In one sentence, state the main point the writer is making in the passage. [5 marks]

5 marks: The market is a centre of trade where goods are bought and sold and prices set. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: It is a place for social contact / meeting friends and relatives. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: It spreads news and information. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: It provides employment for many people besides traders. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: It has religious and cultural significance. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
5 marks: The market is much more than a place for buying and selling. (3 for the correct point, 2 for a clear, complete sentence)
